title: Content Rewards: CPM, Per-Post and Retainer Campaigns Explained
summary: Compare Content Rewards payment models, including Pool campaigns. Work through changing payout shares, approval timing and the costs behind a Whop clipping brief.
body_markdown:
Content Rewards offers CPM, per-post, retainer and Pool campaigns. The choice changes both the work you commission and the uncertainty a creator takes on. A Pool divides an available amount among qualifying participants, so a rising view count can accompany a falling estimated payout. The cheapest headline rate can still be the most expensive campaign to operate.


**Terms checked October 15, 2026.** The current creator and organization terms are dated October 4. People also search for this service as “Whop clipping.” Content Rewards operates the marketplace; Whop handles payments. Legacy Whop-hosted campaigns can retain their prior terms.[Creator terms](https://contentrewards.com/terms) ,[organization terms](https://contentrewards.com/brands-terms)


## What are you actually buying?


Start with the unit of work. A brand that wants ten demonstrations of a new app has a different problem from a podcast trying to distribute a memorable interview through creator accounts. A team that needs familiar people producing new edits every week has another problem again.


CPM compensates qualifying reach; per-post fits defined deliverables; a retainer fits recurring work. A Pool adds a relative-share decision: are participants comfortable with a reward that depends on others' results as well as their own?


Here is how to make the choice operational:


Model A useful fit What the brief must resolve


CPM A permitted source library with many possible moments and distribution through participating accounts Eligible audience, qualifying views, caps and the end of the earning period


Per-post A launch that needs a defined set of demonstrations or editorial treatments What counts as an acceptable post, revision responsibility and any performance condition


Retainer Recurring collaboration where learning the brand should improve future work Work per cycle, feedback deadlines, acceptance and the next cycle's scope


Pool A shared reward budget where participants accept a variable allocation Qualifying participants, counted views, tracking windows, ending responsibility and estimated versus settled amounts


A per-post campaign can still depend on performance conditions. A retainer still needs acceptance criteria. Treat the model name as the beginning of the contract discussion.


## Why more views can mean a smaller Pool estimate


The October 4 organization terms say the displayed Pool budget includes the organization fee; the remainder is divided by eligible creators' counted-view shares. Minimums can apply. Estimates can change before the Pool ends, and a clip's tracking window ending does not itself end the Pool.[Pool mechanics, sections 5.7–5.9](https://contentrewards.com/brands-terms)


Consider a **hypothetical $900 available for allocation after the organization fee, before creator fees** . At the first observation, your approved clips have 100,000 counted views out of 500,000 eligible views: 20%, or $180 before creator fees. Later, your count reaches 150,000 but the eligible total reaches one million: 15%, or $135. You gained 50,000 views while your estimate fell $45.


This is arithmetic, not a customer result or a forecast. It shows why a Pool estimate should not be entered as contracted revenue. For a creator deciding how much editing time to invest, the question is whether the work is worthwhile across several plausible shares, including a disappointing one.


Keep four fields beside the estimate: your counted views, the eligible total, the amount available for allocation and the observation time. Record final settlement separately. A screenshot without its denominator cannot explain what changed.


For a campaign manager, name the person responsible for ending the Pool and communicating the review schedule before inviting submissions. Otherwise, creators and moderators can be working toward different assumptions about when the campaign is finished.


## Compare campaigns using the same cost boundary


Imagine two **hypothetical** campaigns that each deliver 500,000 qualifying views and incur $1,000 in creator compensation. One needs $300 of internal review and coordination; the other needs $900.


Before platform fees and other costs, their effective costs are $2.60 and $3.80 per thousand qualifying views. The advertised creator rate was $2 in both cases.


The useful calculation is:


**Effective CPM = total cost included in your budget ÷ qualifying views × 1,000.**


Define “total cost” before comparing campaigns. Include creator compensation, platform and payment fees, agency fees, production and moderation costs where applicable. A comparison that includes staff time on one side and excludes it on the other will reward the wrong process.


These examples describe cost after performance is observed. They are not forecasts of how much reach a new budget will buy. They also do not tell you whether the viewers were likely customers.


## Read creator fees and brand fees separately


The creator terms specify a 10% creator fee on CPM and Pool payouts. For per-post and retainer campaigns, that fee is 10% below a $5,000 campaign budget and 0% at or above that budget. A promotional discount can change the applicable offer.[Creator fee schedule](https://contentrewards.com/terms)


The organization terms list a 10% standard platform fee, or 8% for a verified organization, plus separately itemized Whop processing costs. Confirm the funding breakdown in the checkout for the campaign you are creating.[Brand funding and fees](https://contentrewards.com/brands-terms)


A creator's net earnings and a brand's total acquisition cost are different calculations. Keep two records: one for the funded campaign and one for what a participating creator earns after applicable deductions. Do not call either number “the fee” without identifying whose fee it is.


## After the migration: reconcile old work before commissioning more


**Migration guidance checked October 22.** Content Rewards' September 13 help article set October 15 as the deadline to reconnect social accounts; an account left unlinked cannot submit clips after that deadline. Existing approved earnings carried over, while legacy campaign terms can remain different from new campaigns. Pending work still needs review, and an exhausted campaign may need a brand top-up before a newly approved submission can be paid. A legacy payout without a visible clip can be an already-paid record, rather than a new amount owed.[Migration guidance](https://help.contentrewards.com/en/articles/16829642-what-happened-to-your-previous-version-submissions-and-payouts)


For an agency, this calls for a reconciliation pass before buying another batch of distribution. Keep the original submission record and add the current account connection, campaign, approval state, expected amount and actual payment. Separate three queues: work awaiting review, approved work awaiting payment and records already settled. Do not add all three to outstanding receivables.


If a record appears missing, check campaign and status filters first. Send support the campaign name and clip link when those checks do not resolve it. If an account missed the relinking deadline, confirm the available recovery path with support instead of assuming another upload will repair the record.[Submission and payout troubleshooting](https://help.contentrewards.com/en/articles/16829642-what-happened-to-your-previous-version-submissions-and-payouts)


Give each unresolved item an owner and a next check date. This keeps a platform migration from becoming a disagreement between an editor, a campaign manager and the client about which work was delivered.


## The approval queue is part of the product


A campaign can attract plenty of submissions and still fail operationally. The pattern is familiar: an ambiguous brief creates avoidable edits, the reviewer rejects them for reasons the creator did not know, and the next batch repeats the disagreement.


Write acceptance criteria as observations a moderator can verify. “Make it premium” gives the creator no useful test. “Keep the speaker's qualification in the final sentence and use the approved product name in the first caption” does.


Put enforceable requirements in the platform fields or acknowledged platform notices described in the terms; an external chat alone is insufficient.[Requirements and review rules](https://contentrewards.com/brands-terms)


Use a shared approval vocabulary: wrong source, missing context, caption error, wrong account, missing campaign requirement, or ready to approve. Over time, the rejection mix tells you what to improve in the next brief. “Bad clip” tells you almost nothing.


For recurring CPM, a round normally includes seven earning days and a three-day hold. The first round opens after both approval and the minimum payout requirement are met. Later approval does not extend the earning window. Pool allocation occurs at its end, normally followed by a three-day hold. Funding and validation still apply; withdrawal is separate.[Payout timing](https://contentrewards.com/terms)


Record approval, threshold attainment, earning-window end, round settlement and withdrawal separately. “Ten days after approval” can be the wrong date when a threshold is reached later. Draft approval also does not guarantee final submission approval or payment.[Creator review terms](https://contentrewards.com/terms)


## A clipping campaign brief you can actually use


Write the brief before choosing the promotional headline. This compact structure works as an internal planning document; copy the binding requirements into the campaign itself.


1. **Audience:** Name who should recognize the problem in the clip. For example, independent restaurant owners hiring their first manager.
2. **Source:** List approved recordings and segments. Identify sponsor reads, embargoes and material outside the permission you have.
3. **Editorial requirement:** State the idea the viewer must understand, plus the context that cannot be removed.
4. **Deliverable:** Define duration, format, captions, required brand elements and permitted destination accounts.
5. **Compensation:** State the model, qualifying events, limits and conditions. Separate indicative earnings from a fixed commitment.
6. **Review:** Name the moderator, revision process and expected response window.
7. **Measurement:** Record the post URL, approval, relevant performance and the business action you want to observe.


Our[campaign planning kit](https://overlap.ai/downloads/clipping-campaign-brief.md) gives a longer starting point. Use the[campaign launch guide](https://overlap.ai/blogs/how-to-start-a-clipping-campaign) to decide what your team will operate itself.


## Marketplace distribution or accounts your brand owns?


A marketplace is useful when you want participating creators to distribute the work. It raises an additional question: after the campaign ends, where do the audience and posting history live?


Overlap's[clipping campaign service](https://overlap.ai/clipping-campaigns) operates on customer-owned accounts. Its product workflow brings together clip selection, formatting, captions, approvals and publishing. That makes it relevant when the goal is to build a repeatable operation around your own catalog and channels.


For a hybrid plan, keep the account roles explicit. A podcast could run regular clips on its own channels and commission a separate marketplace campaign around a particular guest or release. Use separate URLs or other agreed attribution methods where possible, and report each distribution route separately. Views from a creator's account should not be presented as followers gained on the show's account.


See the[Overlap product workflow](https://overlap.ai/product-overview#clipping-workflow) for a finished clip and the steps behind the production process. If the operational model is the decision you are making,[compare clipping agency alternatives](https://overlap.ai/clipping-agency-alternative) before comparing rate cards.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### Is the lowest CPM campaign always the best value?


No. Review costs, audience fit and the business result matter. Compare the same cost categories and qualifying-view definition across campaigns, then check whether the audience did anything useful beyond watching.


### Does a per-post payment mean every submitted clip gets paid?


No. A submission and an accepted deliverable are different things. Read the campaign's approval and performance conditions before producing work.


### Should an agency use a retainer for every recurring campaign?


Use a retainer when the repeated work and feedback cycle can be specified. If the goal is open-ended distribution by many accounts, a different payment structure may fit better. Decide from the operation you need to run.
